newsitem.title: UK: BT clouds merger deal with MCI.
newsitem.headline: BT clouds merger deal with MCI.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc raised analysts' concerns on Thursday about details of its planned $20 billion merger with America's MCI -- some of which have not have been published.

Some analysts said it was becoming increasingly likely that the proposed merger would go ahead -- possibly towards the end of next month -- on unchanged terms because BT wants to avoid being sued by MCI.

Fresh worries have been raised about whether BT might have unwittingly signed into a deal which rules out renegotiation of the merger terms because of difficulties in North America's $100 billion local phone markets.

Since MCI announced an unexpectedly hefty loss forecast in its expanding local business three weeks ago, BT's chairman Sir Iain Vallance has told shareholders that no such separate, secret letter had been signed.

But BT told analysts on Thursday that in a thorough review of both MCI's local and core long-distance operations, it was also looking at the whole agreement again -- parts of which had not been published because they contained confidential commerical information.

BT, which announced first quarter profits on Thursday, declined to comment on whether there was any part of the agreement, published or unpublished, which disallows a fresh deal because of problems in MCI's local business.
"We are dealing with very, very complex legal issues and the danger is that simplistic information could well be inaccurate," a BT spokesman said.
"But we have published those bits of the agremeent which the rules say we have to publish and we haven't published those which the rules say we don't have to."

One analyst noted that details about MCI's plans for breaking further into the lucrative U.S. local markets, which will ring up $800 million of losses this year alone, might have been considered commercial secrets.
"I don't want to say BT were being disingenuous (at the meeting) but they certainly weren't clear," he said.
"The lack of a firm denial of any secret side letter suggests that there is something in it. But there is just not enough information out there."

"If there is no secret agreement why try and cloud the issue more?" asked another analyst. "I think they are going to go forward with the deal without renegotiating it because they are worried about MCI's lawyers."

MCI, which has made no secret of the fact that it wants BT's financial muscle to help it expand into lucrative new markets, is expected to fight "tooth and nail" to ensure the merger will go ahead unchanged.

But analysts also say BT, which wants to create one of the world's most comprehensive global companies, called Concert Plc, to sell communications to high-margin multinational customers, needs access to America. And most analysts say buying MCI, despite the profit warning, is still its best option.

"It's classic poker," said one analyst. "BT's got the money and MCI needs the money. MCI's got the customers and the base in the U.S. and BT needs that. They really can't go back. If this merger falls apart it will fall apart completely."
Oliver Ehrenberg, telecoms analyst at Robert Fleming, was quick to point out that MCI's core long-distance business is also not doing well.
On a rolling 12 month average, call volume growth over the last five quarters has come in at 14.5 percent, 11 percent, 13 percent, 4.0 percent and 5.5 percent in the last quarter.

"This is not particularly impressive given the U.S. economy is more buoyant at the moment than it has been for some time and baby bells (local U.S. operators) haven't entered the long-distance market yet," he said.

BT, whose shares were trading at 424p, a loss of 6.5p, earlier reported a 1.4 percent rise in first quarter pre-tax profits to 881 million pounds ($1.4 billion). But earnings are set to fall until 2000 if, as expected, the merger goes ahead. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
